title: Experts unveil the one country with the longest lifespan – but there's a surprising catch
summary: A 2023-based analysis of 204 countries finds Singapore has the highest life expectancy, with average citizens expected to live beyond 85. However, Singaporeans spend many of their final years in poor health — about 11.2 years on average. The study highlights a widening "morbidity gap": lifespan is rising faster than healthy life expectancy worldwide, driven largely by musculoskeletal, mental, sensory, injury and non-communicable diseases.
content:
Scientists calculated the lifespan of 204 countries.

Living longer doesn't necessarily mean living healthier. Despite having the world's highest life expectancy, people in Singapore spend many of their later years in poor health, according to new research published in The Lancet Public Health.

The study used 2023 data to estimate lifespans in 204 countries and found that Singapore topped the leaderboard, with the average citizen expected to live beyond their 85th birthday.

"Singapore's longevity reflects deliberate long-term policy rather than any single cause," said Dr Marie Ng, associate professor at Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, National University of Singapore (NUS), in an interview with BBC Science Focus. "Its healthcare system, robust social protection and evidence-based governance all allow its citizens to thrive."

The scientists also investigated healthspan: the number of years a person can expect to live in good health. They found that Singaporeans may live well into their 80s, but the last 11.2 years of their lives are likely to be burdened by ill-health.

Researchers call the difference between life expectancy and healthy life expectancy the "morbidity gap". In other words, people are spending more of their lives in poor health than they did in the 1990s.

Global life expectancy rose from 64.6 years in 1990 to 73.8 in 2023, the study found. But healthy life expectancy failed to keep pace, with adults now spending around one in seven years in poor health.

Women typically outlived men, but they also spent more of those extra years in poor health. Globally, the healthspan gap averaged 12.1 years for women, compared with 9.3 years for men. In Singapore the contrast was sharper: although women lived just 4.4 years longer than men, they spent more than twice as many years in poor health — 21.1 years versus 10.4 for men.

Dr Julian Mutz, a research fellow at King's College London who was not involved with the study, noted the persistent "gender health paradox": women live longer but experience more years in poor health. He said the finding underscores a need for more research into why the pattern exists.

People in the US could expect to spend more years in poor health than those in any other country — around 14 years on average — followed closely by Australia and Canada. The study also reported that the gap between lifespan and healthspan seemed to be widening in 203 out of 204 countries, with the single exception of Palestine.

"Most populations now spend a decade or more living in poor health," Ng explained. "For individuals and families, that means more years are spent managing chronic conditions like back pain, hearing loss, neurological disorders and diabetes."

Five groups of conditions accounted for 57.4% of the global morbidity gap in 2023: musculoskeletal disorders (especially low-back pain); mental disorders including depression and anxiety; sense organ diseases such as hearing loss; injuries (especially falls); and non-communicable diseases like diabetes, high blood pressure and heart disease.

Prof Simon Jones from the University of Birmingham's Centre for Musculoskeletal Ageing, who was not involved in the research, said the prominence of musculoskeletal disorders was the most notable finding. "Musculoskeletal disorders were found to be the single biggest contributor to the healthspan gap," he said. "This is a real demonstration of just how important muscles, bones and joints are to healthy ageing."

Ng said the study quantified what many people observe among relatives and older acquaintances. "We have become remarkably good at adding years to life, but far less successful at adding life to those years," she said. The researchers argue the central message is that longevity alone is no longer the right measure of success; policymakers and health systems should focus on improving the quality of those added years.

The study serves as a call to action to shift attention and resources toward interventions that reduce years lived in poor health, from prevention and early treatment of chronic conditions to investments in rehabilitation, hearing care and mental health services. The authors stress that improving healthspan will require coordinated policy, clinical and social responses to the major contributors to the morbidity gap.

Read more: Trends editor Hatty Willmoth.
